newsitem.title: USA: Oil price scare weakening near-term.
newsitem.headline: Oil price scare weakening near-term.

text.p: Heating oil supplies are increasing and prices are coming down, calming the trepidation that led to warnings just a few weeks ago of sharp price increases and possible shortages this winter.
Oil market analysts -- in view of statistics showing an increase of about 5 million barrels of heating oil in the past two weeks -- now believe that prices are heading still lower.
Crude oil futures prices have fallen 8 percent in the past week and heating oil has fallen 11 percent since early in the month.

Crude oil futures were at $24.28 a barrel Wednesday, down from $26.10 last week, which was the highest since the Gulf War. Heating oil futures were at about 68 cents a gallon. Both are traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

"The factors that pulled heating oil and crude up, like Middle East tensions -- specifically in Iraq -- and low heating oil stocks, are now losing their steam," said Paul Ting, senior oil and gas analyst with Salomon Brothers in New York.
"We have started to turn the corner into a market downtrend," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co, a trading firm.

Oil prices had rallied 30 percent from summer lows to last week's peak and heating oil futures rose by 50 percent over the same period, hitting 76.75 cents a gallon in early October, the highest since the middle of the Gulf War in January, 1991.
The heating oil rally was spurred mainly by the low summer build in stocks of distillates, mainly heating oil and diesel, since hitting a record-low 88.4 million barrels in the spring.

Earlier this month Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary met with oil executives to discuss the low heating oil stocks, but analysts say refineries had already stepped up output to take advantage of the higher prices.
"O'Leary did what she had to do, but there was never a question that refiners had already started to maximize heat production," said Bruce Lanni, senior oil analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.

Figures released this week by the Department of Energy and the American Petroleum Institute showed increases of about 5 million barrels of heating oil in the last two weeks in the Northeast, the biggest market for heating oil in the world.
Unseasonably warm weather and replenishing inventories could send heating oil prices down to between 66 cents and 67 cents in the next week or so, market participants said.
Also, some analysts say the Iraqi situation may soon turn bearish for the oil market.

"When the presidential election ends next week, you are going to start to hear talk again of a possible Iraqi deal, so long as Saddam Hussein behaves," said Thomas Blakeslee, an analyst with Cargill Investor Services.

Iraq's intervention in late August to aid one of the warring Kurdish factions led to the suspension by the United Nations of a deal that would have allowed Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months to pay for humanitarian relief.

The Clinton Administration has maintained a tough line on the Iraqi oil deal in the run-up to the November election. But if the deal comes up for discussion again after the Nov. 5 election and with lower heating oil prices, Blakeslee sees crude oil being pushed down to about $23 a barrel.
And if crude supply remains ample in coming months, Brown sees a drop possibly to around $20 a barrel.
